passages.label: Cold open
passages.text:
The sky is a skull.

The clouds are its brain.

The sea is blood, and the mountains are bones.

In Norse myth, the world was a giant once, until three brothers took him apart.

One of them was Odin.

He built everything from a corpse, and then he was told how it would end.

But first, there was nothing at all.

passages.label: A Giant Became The World
passages.text:
Well, almost nothing. Only a great gap, with ice on one side and fire on the other.

Where the cold meets the heat, the ice begins to melt, and out of the drops comes a giant named Eemir.

The skull in the sky is still on his shoulders, for now.

These myths come straight from the sources, so follow the channel for the rest.

Beside him, a cow named Owdhoomla comes out of the same melting ice.

Eemir lives on her milk, and she lives on salty ice.

By the third day, she has licked a whole man out of the ice.

That man's grandsons are Odin and two brothers, Veelee and Vay.

So they kill Eemir.

His blood pours out in such a flood that nearly every frost giant drowns.

The brothers drag the body into the middle of the gap, and build a world out of it.

His flesh becomes the land, and his hair becomes the trees.

His skull becomes the sky, held up by four dwarfs.

Sparks from the fire land are thrown up there as stars.

Not bad for three brothers.

Everything they just built will end in fire.

passages.text:

An eagle sits at the top.

passages.label: The Wolf Everyone Agreed To Chain
passages.text:
Loki is a giant's son who lives among the gods.

He is handsome and charming, and impossible to trust.

In the land of the giants, he has three children.

The first is a wolf named Fenrir.

The second is a serpent named Yormungandr.

The third is a girl named Hel, half dark and half pale.

The gods hear a prophecy that these three will bring them harm, and Odin acts.

He throws the serpent into the deep sea, and it grows until it circles the whole world, biting its own tail.

He sends Hel to the land of the dead, and gives her charge of it.

The gods keep the wolf close, and only Teer dares to feed him.

Fenrir grows fast, so the gods decide to chain him.

They offer him a chain as a game of strength, and he snaps it like thread.

A heavier chain breaks too.

So the gods send to the dwarfs, who make a cord called Glaypneer.

It is made of six things: the sound of a cat's step, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spit.

It looks like a silk ribbon.

Fenrir smells a trick, and agrees on one condition: one of the gods must put a hand in his mouth.

The gods look at one another, and then at the grass.

Teer steps forward, and puts his right hand between the wolf's jaws.

The ribbon goes on, and the harder Fenrir pulls, the tighter it holds.

The gods laugh, all except Teer.

Fenrir bites the hand off, and the wolf stays chained.

That ribbon will not hold forever.

passages.label: The Day Thor Went Fishing For A Serpent
passages.text:
Thor is the god of thunder, strongest of them all, with a hammer named Myolnir.

One day he sets out to find the serpent, disguised as a young man.

He comes to a giant named Heemir, who does not think the stranger will be much use on a boat.

Thor takes the head of the biggest ox on the farm for bait.

They row out, and Heemir says they are far enough, but Thor says row further.

Heemir grows pale.

Thor ties the ox head to a hook, and throws it into the deep, and the serpent bites.

Thor pulls so hard his feet go through the bottom of the boat, and he braces himself on the sea floor.

The serpent rises, and the two of them stare at each other.

Follow the channel to see how this fight ends.

Water pours in, Heemir panics, and Thor lifts his hammer.

Heemir cuts the line.

The serpent sinks back into the sea, and Thor throws the hammer after it.

Thor knocks Heemir overboard, and wades ashore.

Round one is a draw, but they will meet again.

passages.label: The God Nothing Could Hurt
passages.text:
Baldur is the best loved of the gods, so fair and bright that light seems to shine from him.

Then he begins to dream about his own death.

His mother, Frigg, will not take the chance.

She goes to everything in the world and asks for a promise.

Fire, water, iron, stone, trees, sickness, poison, beasts, birds.

Every one swears not to harm Baldur.

The gods are so relieved that they turn it into a game.

Nothing touches him.

Everyone cheers, except Loki.

Loki puts on the shape of a woman and visits Frigg.

He asks if truly everything promised.

Frigg says only one plant, a little mistletoe, was too young to ask.

Loki goes straight out and pulls it up.

How do you hurt a god that nothing can hurt?

At the edge of the game stands the blind god Hod, with nothing to throw.

Loki puts the mistletoe in his hand, and points him at Baldur.

Hod throws.

The mistletoe goes straight through Baldur, and he falls dead.

Odin's son rides to Hel, and begs her to give him back.

She says yes, if every living thing weeps for him.

Everything weeps, even the rocks and the iron, except one giantess, who says she will not.

Some say it was Loki in disguise.

Baldur stays dead.

The gods catch Loki at last, hiding as a salmon.

They bind him to three rocks, and hang a serpent above his face, dripping venom.

His wife, Siggin, sits by his side with a bowl to catch the drops.

When the bowl is full, she has to empty it, and the venom lands on him, and the earth shakes.

Loki will not stay in that cave.

passages.label: Everyone Dies, Then The World Begins Again
passages.text:
The end begins with a winter.

It lasts three winters, with no summer between.

Then wolves swallow the sun and the moon.

The stars go out, the earth shakes, and every chain breaks.

Fenrir runs free, his jaws open from the earth to the sky.

The serpent twists out of the sea, and the waves flood the land.

A ship built of dead men's fingernails sails in.

The sons of Moospel ride from the south, led by Surt, with a flaming sword.

The watchman of the gods, Haymdall, blows his horn.

The gods arm themselves and ride out to the plain.

Odin knows how it ends, and goes anyway.

The wolf goes for Odin and swallows him.

Odin's son Veedar puts one boot on the wolf's jaw, and tears the wolf's throat apart.

Thor meets the serpent at last, and kills it.

Then he walks nine steps, and falls dead from the venom.

Teer and a hound named Garm kill each other.

So do Haymdall and Loki, free at last.

Then Surt flings fire across the earth.

The earth sinks into the sea.

And then, silence.

The earth rises again from the sea, green and new.

Fields grow without anyone sowing them.

A few gods survive, and Thor's sons carry his hammer.

Baldur and Hod come back from the dead.

One man and one woman step out of a forest, where they hid and lived on morning dew.

passages.label: The Christian Who Saved The Gods
passages.text:
So how do we know any of this?

None of this was written down when the poems were first made.

For generations it was recited from memory by poets.

Most of the poems survive in one great book, the Codex Regius, from about twelve seventy.

It was written in Iceland, by Christians, about gods nobody worshipped anymore.

Around twelve twenty, an Icelandic chieftain named Snorry Sturloosun put together a handbook for poets.

Snorri was a Christian too, and his book opens with Adam and Eve, then says the gods were once men from Asia.

Not every source agrees.

In one poem, the makers of the first people have different names.

When they disagree, we follow Snorri.

He was killed in twelve forty-one, on the orders of a Norwegian king.

If this was your kind of story, come back for the next myth.
